The idea that living organisms could spontaneously generate from non-living matter, such as flies from rotting meat, was a concept known as spontaneous generation. This idea was disproven through a series of experiments that demonstrated the need for a pre-existing living organism to produce more living organisms. One of the most famous experiments was conducted by Louis Pasteur in the 19th century.

Pasteur's experiments involved swan-neck flasks that were bent in such a way that any particles or microorganisms that might fall into the liquid would be trapped and unable to reach the liquid. In one experiment, he boiled a mixture of meat broth and gelatin, which would kill any existing microorganisms. After cooling, the flask was sealed, and no microorganisms were observed to develop in the broth. However, when Pasteur created a loop in the neck of the flask, allowing particles to fall into the liquid, microorganisms did develop, proving that the organisms came from the particles that entered the flask, not from the non-living broth itself.

The invention of the microscope was crucial in the development of this understanding because it allowed scientists to see microorganisms that were too small to be observed with the naked eye. Before the microscope, the existence of microorganisms was not well understood, and the concept of spontaneous generation was more plausible. With the microscope, scientists could observe that microorganisms were already present in the environment and that they were responsible for the generation of more microorganisms under the right conditions.

The discovery of the atom and better surgical techniques were not directly related to disproving spontaneous generation. The discovery of the atom contributed to our understanding of the physical world at a very small scale, and better surgical techniques improved medical practices but did not directly address the question of life arising from non-life.

Therefore, the invention of the microscope was the key factor that led to the understanding that living organisms cannot spontaneously generate from non-living matter.
